p2-1.a: EC2: virtual machines you manage; full control, good for legacy or special software.|ECS: run Docker containers as long-running services (on EC2 or Fargate); good for APIs and workers with steady traffic.|Lambda: functions triggered by events, pay per invocation, scale to zero; good for event handlers, glue and spiky workloads, with a 15-minute limit and cold starts.|In IRT we ran microservices on ECS behind load balancers and used Lambda for event-driven pieces.
p2-1.qa: I use ECS (on Fargate or EC2) for long-running containerised services and workers with steady traffic, Lambda for short, event-driven or spiky work (S3 events, queue triggers, schedules) where pay-per-use and zero servers win, and plain EC2 when I need full control of the OS, special software, or licensing that containers or Lambda cannot handle.
i: Lambda limits: 15-minute max duration, up to 10 GB memory, cold starts, concurrency limits; costly at high steady load.
ECS Fargate: no servers to patch, per-task CPU/memory billing; ECS on EC2 is cheaper at scale and allows GPUs or daemon tasks.
EC2: legacy apps, Windows services with installers, custom agents; you own patching, scaling and AMIs.
Cost rule of thumb: spiky or low traffic favours Lambda; constant high traffic favours containers.
In IRT: .NET APIs and RabbitMQ workers on ECS, Lambda for [event-driven pieces such as S3 file arrival notifications], EC2 for [the on-prem-like deployment nodes and tooling servers].
f: Can Lambda run a full ASP.NET Core API?
Yes, with the Lambda ASP.NET Core hosting adapter, but cold starts and per-request cost need checking.
Fargate vs ECS on EC2?
Fargate for simplicity; EC2 capacity providers for cost control at scale or special hardware.

p2-2.a: Cluster: logical group of capacity (EC2 instances or Fargate).|Task definition: the blueprint, like a docker-compose file: image, CPU/memory, env vars, ports, IAM task role, log config.|Task: a running instance of the definition; Service: keeps N tasks running, replaces unhealthy ones, registers them with a load balancer target group, and scales.|Images come from ECR; logs go to CloudWatch.
p2-2.qa: An ECS cluster is a logical group of capacity (Fargate or EC2 instances); a task definition is the versioned blueprint (images, CPU, memory, ports, environment, secrets, IAM roles, logging); a task is a running copy of it; a service keeps the desired number of tasks running, replaces failed ones, registers them with a load balancer and performs rolling or blue/green deployments.
i: Two IAM roles: the task execution role (pull images from ECR, write logs, read secrets at start) and the task role (what your code may call, e.g. S3, SQS).
Networking: awsvpc mode gives each task its own ENI and security group.
Deployments: rolling with minimumHealthyPercent/maximumPercent and the deployment circuit breaker with automatic rollback, or CodeDeploy blue/green.
Service auto scaling with target tracking on CPU, memory or ALB request count per target.
Service Connect or Cloud Map for service discovery between services.
Logs via the awslogs driver to CloudWatch Logs, or FireLens.
f: Task role vs execution role?
Execution role is used by ECS to start the task; the task role is assumed by your application code at runtime.
What happens when a task fails its health check?
The service stops it and starts a replacement, and the ALB stops routing to it.

p2-3.a: A managed front door for APIs: routing to Lambda, ECS/HTTP backends or AWS services.|Handles authentication (JWT/Cognito authorizers, Lambda authorizers, IAM), throttling, quotas, request validation, CORS and stages.|REST APIs (feature rich) vs HTTP APIs (cheaper, faster) vs WebSocket APIs.|Logs and metrics go to CloudWatch.
p2-3.qa: API Gateway is a managed front door for APIs: it receives requests, authenticates and authorises them (JWT, Cognito, Lambda authorizers, IAM), throttles and applies usage plans, validates and transforms requests, and routes them to Lambda, HTTP backends or AWS services, with logging and metrics built in.
i: REST APIs (v1) have more features (usage plans, API keys, request validation, caching, WAF); HTTP APIs (v2) are cheaper and faster with JWT authorizers.
Private integrations reach services in a VPC through VPC Link to an NLB or ALB.
Limits: 29-second default integration timeout (raisable for some APIs), 10 MB payload.
Throttling is token-bucket based per account, stage and method; returns 429.
Custom domains, stages (dev, uat, prod), canary releases per stage.
f: API Gateway or ALB?
API Gateway for API management and serverless; ALB for container services with high steady traffic (Part 5 has the table).
How do you secure it?
JWT/OAuth authorizers, WAF, resource policies, throttling and mutual TLS where needed.

p2-4.a: A cold start happens when AWS must create a new execution environment: download code, start the runtime, run init code.|.NET can have larger cold starts; reduce with smaller packages, native AOT or ReadyToRun, SnapStart where supported, and lighter init.|Provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm for latency-critical paths.|Reuse SDK clients and connections outside the handler.
p2-4.qa: A cold start is the extra latency when Lambda creates a new execution environment: download code, start the runtime, run initialisation, then the handler. It happens on the first request, after idle periods and when scaling out. Reduce it with smaller packages, less work at init, more memory (more CPU), Provisioned Concurrency, SnapStart and, for .NET, native AOT.
i: .NET options: ReadyToRun or native AOT (`PublishAot`) cut startup a lot; avoid heavy reflection and DI scanning at init.
SnapStart (Java, Python and .NET 8 managed runtime) snapshots the initialised environment and restores it.
Provisioned Concurrency keeps environments warm (costs money); schedule it for business hours.
VPC cold-start penalty was largely fixed by Hyperplane ENIs, but still keep dependencies light.
Initialise SDK clients outside the handler so warm invocations reuse them.
f: Does memory affect cold start?
Yes; CPU scales with memory, so more memory often means faster init and can even reduce cost.
How do you measure it?
The Init Duration field in REPORT log lines, or X-Ray traces.

p2-5.a: Start from access patterns, not entities.|Partition key spreads data and must have high cardinality to avoid hot partitions; sort key enables range queries (begins_with, between).|GSIs and LSIs support extra access patterns; single-table design stores related items together.|Use conditional writes for optimistic concurrency, TTL for expiry, Streams to trigger Lambdas.
p2-5.qa: DynamoDB modelling starts from access patterns, not entities: list every query, choose a partition key with high cardinality and even traffic, a sort key for ranges and ordering, and add GSIs for other patterns. Often several entity types share one table (single-table design) with generic keys like PK = STUDY#42, SK = SITE#7.
i: Item collections: items sharing a partition key can be fetched together with one Query.
Avoid scans; every request should be GetItem or Query by key.
Hot partitions: spread writes with sharded keys if one key gets most traffic.
Item limit 400 KB; large payloads go to S3 with a pointer.
Use conditional writes for idempotency and optimistic locking (version attribute), TTL for expiry, Streams for change events.
c:
PK            SK                  Attributes
IDEMP#a1b2    REQ                 status=Done, response=..., ttl=1718000000
STUDY#42      SITE#007            name, country
STUDY#42      SHIPMENT#2024-06-01#881   status, kitCount
f: Single-table design always?
No; it optimises known patterns but is hard to evolve; separate tables are fine for simple cases.
Query vs Scan?
Query reads one partition by key; Scan reads the whole table and is slow and expensive.

p2-6.a: Cache-aside (lazy loading): read cache, on miss read DB and populate; most common.|Write-through: write to cache and DB together; read-heavy consistency.|Write-behind: write to cache, flush to DB later; fast but risky.|Set TTLs, invalidate on change, avoid stampedes with locking or jitter, never cache sensitive patient data without controls.
p2-6.qa: The main patterns are cache-aside (app reads cache, on miss loads from DB and stores it), read-through, write-through (write cache and DB together), write-behind (write cache, persist later) and refresh-ahead. ElastiCache (Redis or Valkey) is AWS's managed in-memory cache, used for shared caches, sessions, rate limits, distributed locks and token denylists.
i: Cache-aside is the most common and simplest; set TTLs and invalidate on writes.
Stampede protection: locks or HybridCache, jittered TTLs, early refresh.
Eviction policies (allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl) and memory limits must be set deliberately.
Redis replication with Multi-AZ failover; cluster mode for sharding.
Never cache without a plan for invalidation and consistency.
In IRT: [study configuration and reference data] cached; the logout fix used ElastiCache for the jti denylist with TTLs.
f: Redis vs Memcached?
Redis has data structures, persistence options, replication and pub/sub; Memcached is simpler, multithreaded, cache-only.
What is a hit ratio?
The share of reads served from cache; monitor it to judge if caching works.

p2-7.a: Application Load Balancer: layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS), path/host routing, header rules, works with ECS target groups and WAF.|Network Load Balancer: layer 4 (TCP/UDP), ultra-low latency, static IPs, millions of requests per second.|Both do health checks and spread traffic across availability zones.|For REST microservices on ECS, ALB is the usual choice.
p2-7.qa: ALB (Application Load Balancer) works at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC): routing by path, host, headers and query, TLS termination, redirects, OIDC authentication and WebSockets. NLB (Network Load Balancer) works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS): extreme throughput, very low latency, static IPs/Elastic IPs and source IP preservation.
i: ALB targets: instances, IPs, Lambda; NLB targets: instances, IPs and even an ALB.
Use NLB for non-HTTP protocols, PrivateLink services, or when clients need fixed IPs.
API Gateway private integrations (REST APIs) need an NLB via VPC Link.
Health checks: ALB uses HTTP paths; NLB can use TCP or HTTP.
Gateway Load Balancer is the third type, for inline appliances (firewalls).
f: Which one for your .NET APIs?
ALB, for path routing to several ECS services and HTTP health checks.
Can ALB give static IPs?
Not directly; put an NLB or Global Accelerator in front.

p2-8.a: S3 is durable object storage: files, exports, backups, static sites, build artifacts.|Storage classes trade cost for access speed; lifecycle rules move or expire objects.|A presigned URL gives time-limited access to upload or download one object without exposing credentials.|Block public access, encrypt with SSE-KMS, and use bucket policies with least privilege.
p2-8.qa: S3 is durable object storage (eleven nines durability) used for files, backups, data lakes, static websites, logs and artifacts. A presigned URL grants temporary access to one object operation (GET or PUT) using the signer's permissions, so clients can download or upload directly to S3 without AWS credentials and without passing through your API.
i: Presigned URLs expire (up to 7 days with IAM user credentials, shorter with temporary credentials); keep them short (minutes).
Uploads: presigned PUT or POST (POST policies can restrict size and content type); multipart for large files.
Storage classes and lifecycle rules (Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier) cut cost.
Security: Block Public Access, bucket policies, SSE-KMS, versioning, Object Lock for WORM retention (useful for GxP evidence).
Events: S3 notifications to Lambda, SQS or EventBridge trigger processing.
f: Who can use a presigned URL?
Anyone who has it until it expires, so treat it like a short-lived secret.
Why upload directly to S3?
It offloads large transfers from your API, avoiding timeouts and memory pressure.

p2-9.a: Give each service its own IAM role (ECS task role, Lambda execution role) with only the actions and resources it needs.|No long-lived access keys in code; use roles and Secrets Manager or Parameter Store.|Use conditions, resource ARNs, and review with IAM Access Analyzer.|Separate accounts or environments for dev, validation and production.
p2-9.qa: Least privilege means every identity gets only the actions on the specific resources it needs, nothing more. I do it with roles (not users) for workloads, narrow policies scoped by resource ARN and conditions, separate roles per service, permission boundaries and SCPs as guardrails, and I refine policies with IAM Access Analyzer and CloudTrail data.
i: Start from AWS managed policies only for prototypes; move to customer-managed, resource-scoped policies.
Conditions: aws:SourceVpce, aws:PrincipalTag, kms:EncryptionContext, time or MFA requirements.
Access Analyzer generates policies from actual CloudTrail activity and finds public or cross-account access.
SSO (IAM Identity Center) for people with short-lived credentials; no long-term access keys.
Separate AWS accounts per environment limit blast radius.
f: Identity-based vs resource-based policies?
Identity policies attach to users and roles; resource policies attach to resources (S3 buckets, KMS keys) and can grant cross-account access.
How do explicit denies work?
An explicit Deny anywhere (policy, SCP, boundary) always wins over Allows.

p2-10.a: A VPC across at least two availability zones.|Public subnets hold the load balancer and NAT gateway; private subnets hold ECS tasks, Lambdas in VPC, RDS and ElastiCache.|Security groups allow only needed ports (ALB to service, service to DB).|VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB keep traffic off the internet.
p2-10.qa: A typical layout is a VPC across at least two availability zones with public subnets for load balancers and NAT gateways, private subnets for ECS tasks and Lambda, and isolated database subnets for RDS and ElastiCache; security groups allow only the needed flows (ALB to app, app to database), and VPC endpoints keep AWS traffic private.
i: Ingress: Route 53, CloudFront/WAF, ALB or API Gateway in public subnets.
Egress: NAT gateway per AZ for internet calls; gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB (free), interface endpoints for ECR, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch.
Security groups reference each other (app SG allows from ALB SG) instead of IP ranges.
Connectivity to on-prem or other VPCs: Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect, Transit Gateway.
VPC Flow Logs for network troubleshooting and audit.
f: Why NAT per AZ?
So one AZ failure does not cut outbound access for the others, and to avoid cross-AZ data charges.
How do private tasks pull ECR images without NAT?
Interface endpoints for ECR API and Docker plus the S3 gateway endpoint.

p2-11.a: Cloud resources are defined in versioned files (CloudFormation, Terraform) instead of clicking in the console.|Benefits: repeatable environments, code review, audit trail, drift detection, easy rebuild and disaster recovery.|Very important in regulated work: every change is traceable.|Changes flow through the same CI/CD as application code.
p2-11.qa: Infrastructure as code defines servers, networks, databases and permissions in versioned files (Terraform, CloudFormation, Bicep) that tools apply automatically. It makes environments reproducible and consistent, reviewable through pull requests, auditable, and quick to recreate, removing manual console changes and drift.
i: Declarative (desired state) vs imperative (steps); most IaC tools are declarative.
Benefits in GxP: change history, peer review and repeatable environments support validation.
Plan or change sets show the impact before applying.
Testing IaC: validate, lint (tflint, cfn-lint), policy as code (Checkov, OPA), and plan reviews.
Modules and templates standardise patterns such as "ECS service with ALB and alarms".
f: What is configuration drift?
The real infrastructure differing from the code because of manual changes.
IaC vs configuration management?
IaC provisions resources; tools like Ansible configure software on them (with overlap).

p2-12.a: CloudFormation: AWS-native, JSON/YAML templates, state managed by AWS as stacks, change sets, rollback on failure.|Terraform: multi-cloud HCL, providers for many services, explicit state file, plan/apply workflow, rich module ecosystem.|CloudFormation gets new AWS features via AWS; Terraform is better when you mix clouds or SaaS.|I have used both for ECS, Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB and RDS resources.
p2-12.qa: CloudFormation is AWS's native IaC service: JSON/YAML templates, state managed by AWS in stacks, change sets, drift detection and day-one support for many AWS features. Terraform is HashiCorp's multi-cloud tool using HCL with providers for AWS, Azure and many SaaS tools, an explicit state file, a large module ecosystem and plan/apply workflow.
i: State: CloudFormation stores it for you; Terraform needs a remote backend (S3 with locking).
Rollback: CloudFormation rolls back failed stacks automatically; Terraform stops and leaves partial changes to fix forward.
Abstractions: CDK generates CloudFormation from TypeScript or C#; Terraform has modules and CDKTF.
Licensing: Terraform moved to the Business Source License in 2023; OpenTofu is the open-source fork.
In IRT [core stacks were in CloudFormation and newer tooling in Terraform]; Part 9 explains why both.
f: Which would you choose for a new AWS-only project?
Either works; CloudFormation/CDK for AWS-native teams, Terraform if multi-cloud or SaaS resources matter.
What is a change set?
A preview of what a CloudFormation update will add, modify or replace.

p2-13.a: State maps resources in code to real resources and stores attributes.|Keep it remote (S3 backend with DynamoDB locking or Terraform Cloud), encrypted, never in Git.|Locking prevents two applies at once; workspaces or separate states per environment.|Use `terraform import` for existing resources and `state mv` for refactors.
p2-13.qa: Terraform state is a JSON file mapping your configuration to real resource IDs and attributes; Terraform uses it to plan changes. I keep it in a remote backend (S3 with versioning and encryption, with DynamoDB or S3 native locking), one state per environment and component, with access restricted because state can contain secrets.
i: Locking prevents two applies corrupting state.
terraform state mv/rm and import blocks refactor or adopt resources without destroying them.
Smaller states (per component) reduce blast radius and speed up plans.
Never edit state by hand; never commit it to Git.
Outputs and terraform_remote_state or data sources share values between states.
f: What if state is lost?
Terraform forgets resources; restore from S3 versioning or re-import (Part 6 has the detail).
Why separate states per environment?
An apply in dev can never touch production resources.

p2-14.a: Write HCL, then `terraform init` to download providers and configure the backend.|`terraform plan` shows the diff; review it in the pull request.|`terraform apply` makes the change after approval.|Run from the pipeline, not laptops; detect drift with scheduled plans.

p2-14.qa: The workflow is write, init, plan, apply: write HCL, `terraform init` downloads providers and configures the backend, `terraform plan` shows the diff between code, state and reality, and `terraform apply` executes the reviewed plan. In pipelines the plan is saved, reviewed in the pull request, approved and then applied exactly.
i: fmt and validate in CI; tflint and Checkov for best practices and security.
`terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `terraform apply tfplan` guarantees what was reviewed is what runs.
Destroy or replace actions (-/+) need extra scrutiny.
Lock provider versions (.terraform.lock.hcl) and module versions.
Run per environment with separate backends and tfvars.
f: What does refresh do?
Updates state from real infrastructure; plan does it by default.
Who can apply to production?
Only the pipeline identity after approval, not individuals from laptops.

p2-15.a: Drift is when real infrastructure no longer matches code, usually from manual console changes.|Detect: CloudFormation drift detection or scheduled `terraform plan`.|Prevent: restrict console write access, all changes through pipelines, tag resources managed by IaC.|Fix: import the change into code or re-apply code.
p2-15.qa: Drift is when real infrastructure no longer matches the IaC code, usually from manual console changes, hotfixes or other tools. I avoid it by making the pipeline the only way to change infrastructure (read-only console access), detecting it regularly (scheduled terraform plan, CloudFormation drift detection, AWS Config rules) and fixing it by updating code or re-applying.
i: Use lifecycle ignore_changes only for fields legitimately managed elsewhere (desired count changed by autoscaling).
Emergency changes are allowed but must be back-ported to code within a set time.
Tag resources with "managed-by" so manual resources stand out.
Alerts when scheduled plans show changes.
f: Drift detected in production: overwrite or adopt?
Understand why first; if the manual change was correct, put it in code; otherwise apply code to restore.
How does ECS autoscaling cause false drift?
The desired count changes; ignore it in Terraform so plans stay clean.

p2-16.a: An image is an immutable, layered template; a container is a running instance of it.|A Dockerfile lists steps: base image, copy files, restore, build, set entrypoint.|Layers are cached, so order instructions from least to most frequently changing.|Containers make dev, test and production behave the same.
p2-16.qa: An image is an immutable, layered template containing the app and its filesystem; a container is a running instance of an image with its own writable layer, process and network. A Dockerfile is the recipe of instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, ENV, EXPOSE, USER, ENTRYPOINT) that builds the image layer by layer.
i: Layers are cached and shared; order instructions from least to most frequently changing.
Images are identified by digest (sha256), tags are movable labels; deploy by digest or immutable tags.
Containers share the host kernel, unlike VMs, so they start in milliseconds.
OCI standard means images run on Docker, containerd, ECS, Kubernetes alike.
f: Container vs VM?
Containers isolate processes and share the kernel; VMs virtualise hardware with their own OS.
Why are images immutable?
Reproducibility: the same image runs identically in every environment.

p2-17.a: Multi-stage build: SDK image to restore and publish, small runtime (aspnet or chiseled) image to run.|Copy csproj files and restore first to cache dependencies.|Run as non-root, expose the port, add a health check endpoint, no secrets in the image.|Tag images with the build/release version and scan them for vulnerabilities.
p2-17.qa: A production .NET Dockerfile is multi-stage: build and publish with the SDK image, then copy only the published output into a small runtime image (aspnet, Alpine or chiseled), run as a non-root user, expose port 8080, set health checks in the orchestrator, and keep secrets out of the image.
i: Copy the .csproj files and restore first to cache NuGet restore layers.
.NET 8+ images run on port 8080 and include a non-root `app` user (`USER $APP_UID`).
Chiseled Ubuntu images have no shell or package manager: smaller and fewer CVEs.
.dockerignore excludes bin, obj, .git and secrets.
Pin base image versions or digests; scan with Trivy in CI.
c:
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY ["Shipments.Api/Shipments.Api.csproj", "Shipments.Api/"]
RUN dotnet restore "Shipments.Api/Shipments.Api.csproj"
COPY . .
RUN dotnet publish "Shipments.Api/Shipments.Api.csproj" -c Release -o /app --no-restore

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0-noble-chiseled
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app .
USER $APP_UID
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "Shipments.Api.dll"]
f: How do you debug a chiseled container without a shell?
Use logs, a sidecar or ephemeral debug container, or a debug image variant in non-production.
Why multi-stage?
The SDK and source never reach the final image, making it smaller and safer.

p2-18.a: Pod: smallest unit, one or more containers sharing network and storage.|Deployment: desired number of pod replicas, rolling updates and rollbacks (via ReplicaSets).|Service: stable virtual IP/DNS that load-balances across pods; Ingress: HTTP routing from outside.|ConfigMap and Secret for configuration; Namespace for isolation; HPA for autoscaling.
p2-18.qa: The core Kubernetes objects are Pod (one or more containers sharing network and storage), Deployment (declares replicas and rolling updates through ReplicaSets), Service (stable virtual IP and DNS for a set of pods), Ingress (HTTP routing from outside), ConfigMap and Secret (configuration), Namespace (isolation), plus StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job/CronJob, PersistentVolumeClaim and HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
i: Labels and selectors connect objects: a Service finds pods by labels.
Controllers continuously reconcile actual state to desired state.
StatefulSet gives stable identities and storage (databases, brokers); DaemonSet runs one pod per node (log agents).
Gateway API is the newer, more expressive successor to Ingress.
RBAC (Role, RoleBinding, ServiceAccount) controls who can do what.
f: Pod vs container?
A pod is the scheduling unit and can hold several tightly coupled containers (sidecars).
Why not create pods directly?
Bare pods are not recreated if they die; Deployments manage them.

p2-19.a: apiVersion, kind: Deployment, metadata (name, labels).|spec.replicas, spec.selector matching pod labels, and spec.template with containers: image, ports, env, resources (requests/limits).|Liveness and readiness probes; strategy (RollingUpdate with maxSurge/maxUnavailable).|A separate Service YAML selects pods by label.
p2-19.qa: A Deployment YAML declares the replica count, the label selector, and the pod template: container image and tag, ports, environment from ConfigMaps and Secrets, resource requests and limits, liveness, readiness and startup probes, security context, and the update strategy (maxSurge, maxUnavailable).
i: Requests drive scheduling and autoscaling; limits cap usage (memory limit breach = OOMKilled).
Probes gate traffic and restarts; readiness must reflect real ability to serve.
securityContext: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop capabilities.
Graceful shutdown: terminationGracePeriodSeconds and a preStop hook so load balancers drain.
Templating with Helm or Kustomize per environment.
f: Should you set CPU limits?
Many teams set only CPU requests, because CPU limits cause throttling; memory limits are essential.
What does maxUnavailable 0 mean?
Never go below the desired replicas during a rollout.

p2-20.a: Readiness: is the pod ready for traffic? If not, it is removed from the Service endpoints.|Liveness: is it stuck? If it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container.|Startup: gives slow-starting apps time before liveness checks begin.|In ASP.NET Core expose /health/ready and /health/live with Health Checks.
p2-20.qa: A liveness probe asks "is the process healthy, or should it be restarted?"; a readiness probe asks "can it receive traffic right now?", and failing removes the pod from load balancing without restarting it; a startup probe protects slow-starting apps by disabling the other probes until startup succeeds.
i: Liveness must be cheap and only check the process itself; checking the database in liveness causes restart storms when the DB blips.
Readiness can check critical dependencies and warm-up state.
ASP.NET Core health checks: tag checks and map /health/live and /health/ready with predicates.
ECS has container health checks and ALB target health checks with similar roles.
f: What happens if readiness fails on all pods?
The Service has no endpoints, so requests fail; that is why readiness checks must be well designed.
Why a startup probe?
So a slow start (migrations, cache warm-up) is not killed by the liveness probe.

p2-21.a: ConfigMap holds non-sensitive config; Secret holds sensitive values (base64, not encrypted by default; enable encryption at rest or use an external secret store).|Inject as environment variables or mounted files.|Keep the same image across environments and change only config.|On AWS, prefer Secrets Manager or Parameter Store integrated with ECS or the cluster.
p2-21.qa: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration; Secrets hold sensitive values (base64-encoded, not encrypted by default, so enable encryption at rest and RBAC). Containers receive both as environment variables or mounted files; in AWS I prefer pulling secrets from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store (ECS secrets, External Secrets Operator or the CSI driver) so they are rotated and audited centrally.
i: 12-factor: configuration via environment, same image for every environment.
Mounted files update when the ConfigMap changes (env vars do not); apps can watch files.
Immutable ConfigMaps improve performance and avoid accidental changes.
Never bake secrets into images or Git; scan for leaks.
In ECS: task definition environment for config, `secrets` referencing Secrets Manager ARNs for credentials.
f: Is a Kubernetes Secret secure?
Only with encryption at rest, RBAC and no broad read access; base64 is encoding, not encryption.
How does .NET read nested config from env vars?
Double underscore: Sftp__Vendors__DepotA__Host.

p2-22.a: Kubernetes HPA scales pod replicas on CPU, memory or custom metrics; Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter adds nodes.|ECS Service Auto Scaling uses target tracking (for example 60 percent CPU) or step scaling from CloudWatch alarms.|Set requests/limits properly or scaling decisions are wrong.|Scale on queue depth for consumers.
p2-22.qa: Kubernetes scales pods with the HorizontalPodAutoscaler based on metrics (CPU, memory, custom metrics like queue length via KEDA) and scales nodes with the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter; ECS scales tasks with Service Auto Scaling (target tracking on CPU, memory or ALB requests per target, step scaling on CloudWatch alarms) and scales EC2 capacity with capacity providers.
i: Target tracking: "keep average CPU near 60 percent"; the system adds or removes capacity automatically.
Scale on the real bottleneck: queue depth for workers, request count or latency for APIs.
Cooldowns and stabilisation windows prevent flapping; scale out fast, in slowly.
Requests must be set correctly for HPA CPU percentages to make sense.
Scheduled scaling for known peaks; minimum capacity for availability.
f: KEDA?
Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling: scales on external metrics such as RabbitMQ queue length, even to zero.
How do you scale RabbitMQ consumers on ECS?
Step scaling on a CloudWatch metric of queue depth or messages per consumer.

p2-23.a: Docker builds and runs containers on one host.|Kubernetes orchestrates containers across many hosts: scheduling, healing, scaling, service discovery; portable but complex.|ECS is AWS's simpler managed orchestrator, tightly integrated with IAM, ALB and CloudWatch.|We used Docker for images, Kubernetes YAML for some workloads and ECS on AWS.
p2-23.qa: Docker builds and runs containers on a single host; Kubernetes is a portable orchestrator that schedules containers across a cluster with self-healing, scaling, service discovery and a huge ecosystem; ECS is AWS's own simpler orchestrator, deeply integrated with IAM, ALB and CloudWatch, without a control plane to manage.
i: Docker Compose is fine for local development and tests, not production orchestration.
Kubernetes: more power and portability, more complexity (networking, upgrades, add-ons).
ECS: fewer concepts, lower operational load, AWS lock-in.
EKS is managed Kubernetes on AWS; Fargate can run both ECS tasks and EKS pods.
IRT production runs on ECS; Kubernetes is used for [some internal workloads] (see Part 9 for the honest answer).
f: When choose Kubernetes over ECS?
Multi-cloud or on-prem portability, a platform team, or ecosystem needs (operators, service mesh).
Is Docker needed on Kubernetes nodes?
No; Kubernetes uses containerd or CRI-O; Docker-built images still run because they are OCI images.

p2-24.a: Continuous integration: every merge builds and runs tests automatically.|Continuous delivery: every build is releasable; production deploy is a manual approval.|Continuous deployment: every passing change goes to production automatically.|In a regulated GxP product we do continuous delivery with formal approval gates.
p2-24.qa: Continuous integration means every change is merged often and automatically built and tested; continuous delivery means every passing build is releasable and deployment to production is a push-button decision; continuous deployment goes further and deploys every passing change to production automatically, with no manual gate.
i: CI needs fast, reliable tests and trunk-based or short-lived branches.
Continuous delivery fits regulated products: automated up to production, with human approval and change control before release.
Continuous deployment needs strong automated tests, feature flags, monitoring and automatic rollback.
DORA metrics measure delivery: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore.
f: Which does IRT use?
Continuous integration and continuous delivery with formal FV, UAT and production approvals.
How do feature flags help?
They separate deploying code from releasing features, so incomplete work can ship turned off.

p2-25.a: Build pipeline (YAML): restore, build, unit tests, SonarQube analysis and quality gate, publish artifacts and Docker images.|Release: deploy the same artifact through environments: FV (validation), TechOps, UAT, then production.|Each stage has approvals and checks; Ansible, Python and Shell scripts run the multi-node installs.|Release is merged and tagged so every environment is traceable to one version.
p2-25.qa: A YAML build pipeline triggers on pull requests and merges: restore, build, unit tests with coverage, SonarQube analysis and quality gate, dependency scanning, publish versioned artifacts and Docker images. The release then promotes the same artifact through FV, TechOps, UAT and production with approvals and checks at each stage, using Ansible, Python and Shell scripts for multi-node installs, and every environment traces back to one tagged version.
i: Branch policies require a green build and reviewers before merge.
Versioning: semantic version plus build number and commit hash stamped into the artifact.
Environment approvals and checks (business hours, change request id) in Azure DevOps environments.
Post-deploy verification: version check on every node, health endpoints and smoke tests.
Since [2025] most deployments are driven through the CIRT MCP server, which triggers the same releases.
c:
trigger: { branches: { include: [ main, release/* ] } }
stages:
- stage: Build
  jobs:
  - job: build
    steps:
    - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2
      inputs: { command: test, projects: '**/*Tests.csproj', arguments: '--collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"' }
    - task: SonarQubeAnalyze@6
    - task: PublishPipelineArtifact@1
      inputs: { targetPath: '$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)', artifact: 'drop' }
f: How do you make sure production gets exactly what was tested?
Build once, promote the same immutable artifact; never rebuild per environment.
What checks run before production?
Approvals by release manager and QA, change request reference, FV and UAT sign-off evidence.

p2-26.a: YAML pipelines live in the repo: versioned, reviewed, templated, multi-stage.|Classic Releases are configured in the UI with visual stages and approvals; common on on-prem Azure DevOps Server.|YAML supports environments with approvals and checks; templates remove duplication.|Our MCP server talks to Azure DevOps Server APIs to trigger and monitor both builds and releases.
p2-26.qa: YAML pipelines define build and deployment as code in the repository (versioned, reviewed, branchable, reusable templates, multi-stage with environments and checks); classic release pipelines are configured in the web UI with a visual designer, which is easier to start with but harder to review, version and reuse. Microsoft's direction is YAML.
i: YAML templates (extends, stage templates) standardise pipelines across many services.
Environments with approvals, checks and deployment history replace classic stage approvals.
Classic still has features some teams rely on (gates UI, release variables per stage, easier artifact triggers), especially on older on-prem Azure DevOps Server.
Migration: export classic definitions and recreate as YAML stages step by step.
On our on-prem Azure DevOps Server we have [YAML builds and some classic release definitions], which the MCP server drives through the REST API.
f: Why does pipeline-as-code matter in GxP?
Pipeline changes are reviewed and versioned like application code, which supports change control.
What is an extends template?
A required base template that pipelines must extend, enforcing mandatory steps such as scans.

p2-27.a: Feature branches off main/develop with pull requests, reviews and build validation.|Release branches cut for a version; hotfix branches from the release tag.|Tags mark exactly what was deployed (semantic version), which auditors and support rely on.|I owned merging and tagging releases across application, APIs, database and UI.
p2-27.qa: We use short-lived feature branches from main merged through pull requests with build validation and reviews, release branches cut for each release (release/2024.3) where only fixes go, hotfix branches from the release tag, and annotated tags marking exactly what was released to each environment so builds are traceable.
i: Fixes on a release branch are merged back to main (or cherry-picked) so they are not lost.
Semantic versions in tags (v2024.3.1) and in artifacts.
Trunk-based development with feature flags is the alternative for faster delivery.
GitFlow's develop branch adds overhead; most teams simplified to main plus release branches.
As release integrator I merge team features, resolve conflicts and create the tags.
f: Why tag releases?
To reproduce exactly what is in production and to compare releases for audit and debugging.
Merge or rebase?
Squash or merge commits for PRs per team convention; never rewrite shared history.

p2-28.a: Ansible automates configuration and installs over SSH or WinRM with no agent, using playbooks and roles in YAML.|We used Ansible with Python and Shell scripts to install releases across multiple nodes.|Idempotent tasks can run many times and leave the same end state (for example 'ensure service is running').|Inventory files define the nodes per environment.
p2-28.qa: Ansible is an agentless automation tool that runs YAML playbooks over SSH or WinRM to configure servers and install software. In IRT our release installs ran through Ansible playbooks with Python and Shell scripts across the multi-node environments; idempotency means running a task again leaves the same end state, so reruns after a failure are safe.
i: Modules are idempotent by design (copy, template, service: state=started); raw shell commands are not unless guarded with creates/removes or changed_when.
Inventories define nodes per environment; group_vars hold environment settings; Ansible Vault encrypts secrets.
Roles organise reusable steps; handlers restart services only when something changed.
--check and --diff do a dry run; serial controls rolling updates across nodes.
The MCP deployment tools trigger the same release stages that run these playbooks.
c:
- name: Deploy shipments service
  hosts: app_nodes
  serial: 1                      # one node at a time
  tasks:
    - name: Copy release package
      ansible.builtin.unarchive: { src: "shipments-{{ version }}.zip", dest: /opt/irt/shipments }
      notify: restart shipments
  handlers:
    - name: restart shipments
      ansible.builtin.service: { name: shipments, state: restarted }
f: Ansible vs Terraform?
Terraform provisions infrastructure; Ansible configures and deploys onto it.
How do you make a shell task idempotent?
Add creates: or a condition, or check state first and set changed_when properly.

p2-29.a: Rolling: replace instances gradually; no extra capacity, but mixed versions run for a while.|Blue-green: deploy to an idle copy, switch traffic at once; instant rollback, double resources.|Canary: send a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, then expand.|Choose by risk, cost and how easily you can roll back.

rows: Switch all traffic to new copy

p2-29.qa: Rolling deployment replaces instances gradually with the new version; blue-green runs a full new environment (green) next to the old (blue) and switches traffic at once, allowing instant rollback; canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watches metrics, then increases gradually.
i: Rolling: cheap and default in ECS/Kubernetes; old and new versions run together briefly, so changes must be backward compatible.
Blue-green: double capacity during the switch; database must work for both versions.
Canary: needs good metrics and automated analysis (Argo Rollouts, CodeDeploy, App Mesh weights).
Feature flags complement all three by decoupling release from deployment.
IRT releases are rolling node by node in controlled windows, with verification after each node.
f: Which is safest for database changes?
Any, if you use expand/contract migrations so both versions work with the schema.
How do you roll back a canary?
Shift traffic back to the stable version automatically when error or latency thresholds break.

p2-30.a: Keep schema changes backward compatible (expand-contract) so the previous app version still works.|Keep the previous artifact and release tag ready to redeploy; feature flags to switch off new behaviour.|Back up before risky migrations; have tested down scripts where feasible.|Define go/no-go checks and smoke tests after deployment.
p2-30.qa: I plan rollback so the application can roll back without rolling back the database: schema changes are backward compatible (expand/contract), applied before the app, and destructive steps happen only in a later release. If a database rollback is really needed, there is a tested down script or a restore point, decided in advance in the release plan.
i: Expand: add columns/tables (nullable or defaulted), deploy app writing both; contract: drop old structures in a later release.
Data migrations are reversible or backed up (copy tables) before running.
Practise rollback in UAT; document the decision criteria and owner.
Feature flags turn off new behaviour without a deployment.
In GxP the rollback plan is part of the change request and approved with it.
f: Why not just restore a backup?
You lose data written since the backup; it is the last resort.
How long do you keep the old columns?
At least one release after the app stops using them, so rollback remains possible.

p2-31.a: Every change links to a requirement or defect, with impact assessment, review and test evidence.|Formal environments and sign-offs: FV, TechOps, UAT, production; segregation of duties.|Validated, repeatable deployment scripts and an audit trail of who deployed what and when.|Automation helps: our MCP-driven deployments kept the steps consistent and logged, while humans kept approvals.
p2-31.qa: In GxP, every release follows change control: documented change requests with impact and risk assessment, traceability from requirements to tests, formal validation (FV) with evidence, independent QA and TechOps installs in qualified environments, UAT sign-off, approved deployment windows, and post-deployment verification, with everything recorded for audit.
i: Separation of duties: developers do not deploy to production themselves.
Only validated artifacts move forward; no rebuilds between environments.
Deviations and incidents are documented with CAPA (corrective and preventive actions).
Automation helps if it is itself controlled and validated (our MCP server keeps approvals in Azure DevOps).
Release cadence is slower and planned; hotfixes still need expedited change control.
f: What is CAPA?
Corrective and Preventive Action: fixing a problem and preventing recurrence, with documentation.
How do you speed things up in GxP?
Automate evidence collection, test early, and keep changes small and well-documented.

p2-32.a: Logs: detailed event records (what happened), structured JSON in CloudWatch Logs.|Metrics: numbers over time (latency, error rate, CPU, queue depth) for dashboards and alarms.|Traces: the path of one request across services, joined by a trace or correlation id.|Together they let you detect, locate and explain issues.
p2-32.qa: Logs are timestamped records of discrete events with detail (errors, requests, business events); metrics are numeric measurements aggregated over time (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, CPU) that are cheap to store and ideal for dashboards and alerts; traces follow a single request across services as a tree of timed spans, showing where time and errors occur.
i: Use metrics to detect, traces to locate, logs to explain.
Correlate them: trace id in logs, exemplars in metrics linking to traces.
Cardinality: avoid high-cardinality labels (user id) in metrics; put those in logs and traces.
OpenTelemetry standardises all three signals.
f: Why not just logs?
Logs are expensive to query at scale and poor for trends; metrics alert faster and cheaper.
What are percentiles?
p95 latency means 95 percent of requests were faster; averages hide slow tails.

p2-33.a: CloudWatch Logs for application logs with Logs Insights queries; metrics from ECS, Lambda, ALB, RDS; alarms to notify on thresholds.|Grafana dashboards combine CloudWatch and other sources into one view for services and releases.|Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency), not just CPU.|After a release, watch dashboards for regressions.
p2-33.qa: CloudWatch is AWS's native monitoring: Logs (with Logs Insights queries), Metrics (AWS and custom), Alarms (with SNS actions), dashboards and X-Ray traces. Grafana is a visualisation layer that queries CloudWatch and other sources (Prometheus, Loki) in one place with richer dashboards and alerting. We use CloudWatch as the data store and Grafana for team dashboards.
i: Logs Insights: `fields @timestamp, @message | filter CorrelationId = "abc" | sort @timestamp`.
Metric filters turn log patterns into metrics (count of "SFTP transfer failed").
Embedded Metric Format lets apps emit metrics through structured logs.
Alarms: composite alarms reduce noise; anomaly detection for seasonal metrics.
Grafana: one dashboard per service with golden signals, plus business panels (shipments processed).
c:
fields @timestamp, level, message, CorrelationId
| filter service = "shipments-api" and level = "Error"
| stats count() by bin(5m)
f: How do you control CloudWatch Logs cost?
Retention policies, sensible log levels, and avoiding verbose debug logs in production.
Where do you look first in an incident?
The service's Grafana dashboard for golden signals, then Logs Insights for errors.

p2-34.a: Latency: how long requests take (track p95/p99, not just average).|Traffic: requests per second or messages per second.|Errors: failure rate (5xx, exceptions, dead-lettered messages).|Saturation: how full the system is (CPU, memory, connection pool, queue depth).
p2-34.qa: The four golden signals from Google's SRE book are latency (how long requests take, separating successes and failures), traffic (demand, such as requests per second), errors (rate of failed requests) and saturation (how full the system is: CPU, memory, queue depth, connection pools). Monitoring them gives a quick health picture of any service.
i: RED method for services: Rate, Errors, Duration; USE method for resources: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors.
Use percentiles (p95, p99) for latency, not averages.
Saturation predicts problems before errors appear (queue growth, pool exhaustion).
Business signals complete the picture (shipments processed per hour).
f: Which signal warns earliest?
Saturation, because queues and pools fill before latency and errors spike.
Why separate failed request latency?
Fast failures (instant 500s) can make average latency look better while things are broken.

p2-35.a: Stabilise first: mitigate impact (rollback, scale, failover) and communicate.|Gather evidence: timeline, dashboards, logs by correlation id, recent changes.|Form and test hypotheses; use 5 Whys to go past the symptom to the real cause.|Fix, add monitoring or tests so it cannot recur, and write a blameless post-mortem.

steps.title: Detect
steps.detail: Alarm or user report; open an incident

steps.title: Investigate
steps.detail: Timeline, dashboards, logs by correlation id, recent changes

p2-35.qa: I start by stabilising (mitigate impact), then build a timeline, gather evidence (metrics, logs, traces, recent changes), form hypotheses and test them one at a time until I find a cause that explains every symptom; then I fix it, verify, and write a blameless post-mortem with actions so it does not recur.
i: Ask what changed: deployments, config, data volume, vendor behaviour, certificates.
5 whys or a fishbone diagram to go from symptom to root cause.
Reproduce in a lower environment when possible.
Distinguish trigger (the event) from root cause (the weakness) and contributing factors.
Example: the RabbitMQ outage: trigger = large vendor file and memory alarm; root cause = publishing without confirms; fix = publisher confirms plus alerts.
f: What is a blameless post-mortem?
A review focused on systems and processes, not individuals, so people share facts openly.
When is RCA complete?
When the cause explains all symptoms, the fix is verified and prevention actions are tracked.

p2-36.a: Actionable: someone knows what to do when it fires; link a runbook.|Based on user impact and sustained thresholds to avoid noise.|Routed to the right owner with severity.|Reviewed regularly; delete alerts nobody acts on.
p2-36.qa: A good alert is actionable (someone must do something now), urgent, tied to user impact or an SLO, has a clear owner and a runbook link, fires rarely when nothing is wrong, and carries enough context (service, environment, dashboard link) to start immediately.
i: Alert on symptoms (error rate, latency SLO burn) rather than every cause (CPU 80 percent).
Use multi-window burn-rate alerts for SLOs to catch fast and slow burns.
Tune thresholds and durations to avoid flapping; review noisy alerts regularly.
Non-urgent issues go to tickets or dashboards, not pages.
Every alert should have a runbook: what it means, how to check, how to mitigate.
f: What is alert fatigue?
Too many low-value alerts make people ignore all alerts, including important ones.
Example of a good alert in IRT?
Shipment status messages in DLQ greater than zero for 10 minutes, linked to the replay runbook.

p2-37.a: RabbitMQ: a message broker with exchanges and queues; messages are removed after acknowledgement; flexible routing; great for task queues and commands.|Kafka: a distributed, partitioned, append-only log; messages are retained and can be replayed; very high throughput; consumer groups track offsets.|Ordering: Kafka per partition; RabbitMQ per queue with one consumer.|Use RabbitMQ for work distribution, Kafka for event streams and integrations needing replay.
p2-37.qa: Kafka is a distributed, append-only log: messages are retained for a period, consumers track their own offsets, many consumer groups can read the same stream and replay it, and ordering is per partition with very high throughput. RabbitMQ is a message broker with queues and flexible routing (exchanges), per-message acknowledgements, priorities and TTLs; messages are removed once consumed.
i: Kafka fits event streaming, multiple independent consumers, replay, audit-like history, analytics.
RabbitMQ fits task queues, commands, request/reply, complex routing, per-message retry and DLQ.
Scaling: Kafka by partitions; RabbitMQ by queues and competing consumers (quorum queues for HA).
RabbitMQ Streams add log-like replay; Kafka adds queue-like features in newer versions (share groups).
In IRT: Kafka for shipment status events consumed by several services; RabbitMQ for notifications and work queues.
f: Which gives ordering?
Kafka per partition (by key); RabbitMQ per queue with a single consumer.
Which is easier to operate?
RabbitMQ for small setups; Kafka is simpler as a managed service (MSK, Confluent).

p2-38.a: A topic is split into partitions; each is an ordered log with offsets.|Producers choose a partition by key, so all events for one key (for example a study id) stay in order.|In a consumer group, each partition is read by exactly one consumer, so parallelism is limited by partition count.|Consumers commit offsets; replication across brokers gives durability.
p2-38.qa: A topic is a named stream of events split into partitions; each partition is an ordered, append-only log stored on brokers and replicated. Producers choose the partition by key (same key, same partition, same order); a consumer group shares the partitions among its consumers so each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group, while different groups read independently.
i: Parallelism is capped by partition count within a group.
Offsets are committed per group and partition; consumers resume from them after restarts.
Rebalancing reassigns partitions when consumers join or leave; cooperative rebalancing reduces pauses.
Choose keys for ordering needs (ShipmentId) and even distribution.
Retention by time or size, independent of consumption.
f: Can you reduce partitions?
No; you can only add them, and adding changes key-to-partition mapping for new messages.
What happens with two groups on one topic?
Each group gets every message, so different services can process the same events.

p2-39.a: Direct: routes by exact routing key.|Topic: routes by pattern (`shipment.*.created`).|Fanout: broadcasts to all bound queues.|Headers: routes by header values. Producers publish to exchanges, never directly to queues.
p2-39.qa: RabbitMQ has four main exchange types: direct (routes to queues whose binding key equals the routing key), topic (pattern matching with * for one word and # for zero or more, like shipment.*.delivered), fanout (broadcasts to all bound queues, ignoring keys) and headers (routes on message header values). The default exchange routes directly to the queue named by the routing key.
i: Direct for commands to specific workers; topic for event categories; fanout for broadcast notifications.
Alternate exchanges catch unroutable messages; mandatory flag returns them to the publisher.
Dead-letter exchanges route rejected or expired messages.
Consistent-hash exchange (plugin) spreads by key for sharding.
c:
await channel.ExchangeDeclareAsync("shipments", ExchangeType.Topic, durable: true);
await channel.QueueBindAsync("notify-sites", "shipments", "shipment.*.delivered");
f: Which exchange for "every service gets every event"?
Fanout, or topic with # binding.
What happens to messages with no matching binding?
They are dropped, unless mandatory or an alternate exchange is used.

p2-40.a: By default a publish is fire-and-forget: if the broker is under pressure, restarts or a connection drops, messages can be lost silently.|With publisher confirms the channel is put in confirm mode and the broker acks (or nacks) each message once it is safely handled (persisted for durable queues).|The publisher tracks unconfirmed messages and retries or alerts on nack or timeout.|Combined with durable queues, persistent messages and consumer manual acks, this gives at-least-once delivery.|Situation: [one evening in mid-2024] a production RabbitMQ node hit its memory high watermark while a [large vendor shipment-status file] was being loaded. The broker blocked publishers and dropped some connections, and for [about 40 minutes] shipment-status updates from the vendor integration service never reached the shipment service. Randomization and dispensing were not affected.|Task: I was on the support rotation, so I had to restore the flow, find the root cause and stop it happening again.|Action: Grafana showed the integration service publishing normally while the incoming rate on the shipments queue had dropped to zero. The RabbitMQ management UI showed the memory alarm and blocked connections. The app logs had no errors because we published with BasicPublish and no confirms. To recover, I scaled out consumers to drain the backlog and replayed the missed window from the vendor files, which was safe because consumers upsert status by shipment id. The permanent fix was publisher confirms with tracking of unconfirmed messages, retry with backoff on nack or timeout, persistent messages on durable queues, and alerts on nacks, memory alarms and blocked connections.|Result: the replay recovered all [about 1,200] updates the same evening. In the [12 months] since there has been no silent loss, and a later broker restart produced [a few dozen] nacks that were retried automatically and showed up in alerts. The full STAR version is in part 3.
p2-40.fu: Why did messages vanish without any error?::BasicPublish returns once the bytes are written to the socket. If the connection drops before the broker stores the message, the publisher never finds out. Without confirms there is no signal at all.||Do confirms slow publishing down?::Waiting synchronously after every message would. We track confirms asynchronously against delivery tags, which cost about [5 percent] throughput, an acceptable price for no loss.||Why not switch to Kafka?::RabbitMQ fits our command and work-queue flows. The problem was a missing delivery guarantee, not the broker, and Kafka would need the same discipline (acks=all, retries, idempotent consumers).

messages.note: No ack or a nack within timeout: retry or alert

p2-40.qa: Publisher confirms make RabbitMQ acknowledge each published message once it is safely stored (or nack it), so the publisher knows about failures instead of losing messages silently. In [mid-2024] a memory alarm blocked publishers and dropped connections, and for [about 40 minutes] shipment-status updates vanished without errors because we published without confirms; I recovered by replaying the vendor files (consumers upsert, so it was safe) and fixed it permanently with confirms, retries, alerts and memory tuning.
i: How confirms work: channel in confirm mode, each message gets a delivery tag, broker sends basic.ack or basic.nack; with persistent messages to durable or quorum queues the ack comes after writing to disk.
In RabbitMQ.Client 7, `CreateChannelOptions(publisherConfirmationsEnabled: true, publisherConfirmationTrackingEnabled: true)` makes BasicPublishAsync wait for the confirm and throw on nack.
Track asynchronously in batches to keep throughput; we saw about [5 percent] cost.
Full guarantee chain: durable queues, persistent messages, confirms, manual consumer acks, DLQ, idempotent consumers; plus an outbox for publish-after-commit.
Monitoring added: memory and disk alarms, blocked connections, publish vs deliver rates, and an alert when the incoming rate drops to zero during business hours.
f: What does the memory high watermark do?
When RabbitMQ memory exceeds it (default 40 percent of RAM, or a set value), the broker blocks publishing connections until memory drops.
Confirms vs transactions?
AMQP transactions also give safety but are much slower; confirms are the recommended approach.
wv: I take ownership on support duty: restore service first, then fix the root cause.
I turn an incident into lasting guarantees and monitoring, not just a one-off fix.

p2-41.a: At-most-once: no retries; messages may be lost.|At-least-once: retries until acknowledged; duplicates possible, so consumers must be idempotent. The usual practical choice.|Exactly-once: no loss and no duplicates; only within limits (Kafka transactions) or achieved effectively through idempotency.|Design for at-least-once plus idempotent consumers.
p2-41.qa: At-most-once means a message is delivered zero or one time (may be lost, never duplicated: ack before processing); at-least-once means it is never lost but may be duplicated (ack after processing, retry on failure); exactly-once means each message affects the system once, which in practice is achieved as effectively-once: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
i: Most real systems choose at-least-once with idempotent consumers.
Kafka offers exactly-once semantics inside Kafka (idempotent producer plus transactions for read-process-write).
Across systems (Kafka to database) you need idempotency or storing offsets with the data in one transaction.
At-most-once fits metrics or telemetry where loss is acceptable.
f: Where can duplicates come from?
Producer retries, consumer crashes before committing, redelivery after timeouts.
How do you test idempotency?
Deliver the same message twice in an integration test and assert the state is unchanged.

p2-42.a: Give every message a unique id; store processed ids (inbox table) and skip repeats.|Use natural idempotency: upserts, 'set status to shipped' rather than 'increment'.|Make the processed-id insert and the business update in the same transaction.|Retry with backoff, then dead-letter after N attempts.
p2-42.qa: An idempotent consumer produces the same result if it processes the same message twice. I give every message a unique id and either record processed ids in a table (inbox pattern) in the same transaction as the business change, or design the change itself as an upsert or conditional update (set status where version is older) so repeats are harmless.
i: Inbox table: unique constraint on MessageId; insert fails for duplicates, so skip them.
Natural idempotency: "set shipment 881 to Delivered" is idempotent; "add 10 kits" is not, so carry the target state or a version.
Keep processed-id records for longer than the maximum redelivery window, then clean up.
External side effects (emails, API calls) need their own idempotency keys.
Our shipment consumers upsert status by shipment id, which is why replaying vendor files after the outage was safe.
c:
INSERT INTO dbo.InboxMessages (MessageId, ProcessedAt) VALUES (@MessageId, SYSUTCDATETIME()); -- unique key
UPDATE dbo.Shipments SET Status = @Status, StatusAt = @At
WHERE ShipmentId = @ShipmentId AND (StatusAt IS NULL OR StatusAt < @At);  -- ignore older/duplicate events
f: Why do this in one transaction?
So the business change and the processed marker succeed or fail together.
What about out-of-order messages?
Compare timestamps or versions and ignore stale updates, as in the WHERE clause.

p2-43.a: Messages that keep failing (or expire, or are rejected) are moved to a separate DLQ instead of blocking the main queue.|Alert on DLQ depth, inspect, fix the cause, then replay.|In RabbitMQ configure a dead-letter exchange; in Kafka publish to a retry or DLT topic.|Never silently drop clinical data messages.
p2-43.qa: A dead-letter queue holds messages that could not be processed after retries (or that expired or were rejected), so they do not block the main queue or get lost. Operators inspect them, fix the cause and replay them; alerts fire when the DLQ is not empty.
i: RabbitMQ: queue argument x-dead-letter-exchange; messages rejected with requeue=false, expired by TTL or over a length limit go there; quorum queues add delivery limits.
SQS: redrive policy with maxReceiveCount and DLQ redrive back to the source.
Kafka: dead-letter topic written by the consumer code or the framework.
Store failure reason and attempt count in headers for diagnosis.
Poison messages (always failing) must go to the DLQ quickly instead of retrying forever.
f: What do you do with DLQ messages?
Investigate, fix code or data, then replay them with a tool or script, and document it.
Can retries cause DLQ storms?
Yes, if a dependency is down; use backoff and circuit breakers so transient outages do not dead-letter everything.

p2-44.a: Problem: you update the database and publish an event; if one succeeds and the other fails, systems disagree.|Solution: in the same DB transaction, write the business change and an outbox row.|A background relay reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka or RabbitMQ, marking rows sent (retry until confirmed).|Consumers stay idempotent because the relay may publish twice.
p2-44.qa: The transactional outbox pattern saves the business change and the event to publish in the same database transaction (into an Outbox table); a separate relay then reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes them to the broker, marking them sent. This guarantees an event is published if and only if the change committed, without distributed transactions.
i: Delivery is at-least-once (the relay may publish twice after a crash), so consumers must be idempotent.
Relay options: polling background service, CDC (Debezium reading the transaction log), or libraries (MassTransit, NServiceBus, Wolverine outbox).
Keep ordering per aggregate by publishing in sequence per key.
Clean up old published rows.
Inbox pattern is the consumer-side mirror for deduplication.
f: Why not publish right after SaveChanges?
If publishing fails or the process crashes between the two, the event is lost while the data changed.
Polling vs CDC?
Polling is simple; CDC has lower latency and no polling load but needs more infrastructure.

p2-45.a: Authentication: who are you (login, token validation).|Authorization: what are you allowed to do (roles, claims, policies, resource checks like 'can this user see this study?').|In ASP.NET Core: UseAuthentication then UseAuthorization; [Authorize(Policy = ...)].|401 = not authenticated, 403 = authenticated but not allowed.
p2-45.qa: Authentication answers "who are you?" by verifying identity (password, SSO, token, certificate); authorization answers "what are you allowed to do?" by checking permissions for that identity on a resource or action. In ASP.NET Core, UseAuthentication builds HttpContext.User and UseAuthorization enforces policies; failures return 401 and 403 respectively.
i: Role-based (RequireRole), claims-based and policy-based authorization; resource-based for "this user on this study".
Authorization must happen on the server for every request; UI hiding is not security.
Least privilege and separation of duties (e.g. unblinded vs blinded roles in clinical trials).
OAuth 2.0 is about delegated authorization; OpenID Connect adds authentication.
f: 401 Unauthorized actually means unauthenticated; 403 Forbidden means authenticated but not permitted.
Where do you check "user can access this study"?
In a resource-based authorization handler, using the study id from the request.

p2-46.a: Three base64url parts: header (algorithm), payload (claims: sub, roles, exp, iss, aud), signature.|The API validates signature with the issuer's key, plus issuer, audience, expiry and not-before.|It is signed, not encrypted: never put secrets or PHI in it.|Keep access tokens short-lived; use refresh tokens to get new ones.

rows: sub, roles, iss, aud, exp, jti

p2-46.qa: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, signed token with three Base64URL parts: header (algorithm, key id), payload (claims such as sub, iss, aud, exp, roles) and signature. The API validates it by checking the signature with the issuer's public key (from JWKS), then issuer, audience, expiry and not-before, and only then trusts the claims.
i: Signed is not encrypted: anyone can read the payload, so never put secrets or PHI in it (JWE exists for encryption).
Reject alg "none" and enforce expected algorithms (RS256/ES256); never let the token choose a symmetric key.
Short lifetimes plus refresh tokens; revocation needs extra measures (our jti denylist).
Key rotation via kid and JWKS caching.
ASP.NET Core JwtBearer does all this; Part 10 shows the pipeline.
f: Access token vs ID token?
The access token is for APIs; the ID token tells the client app who logged in and must not be sent to APIs.
Where should a SPA store tokens?
In memory with a BFF or HttpOnly cookies, not localStorage.

p2-47.a: The app redirects the user to the identity provider with a code challenge.|User logs in (SSO); IdP redirects back with a short-lived authorization code.|The app exchanges the code plus the code verifier for tokens: access token (OAuth, for APIs) and ID token (OIDC, who the user is).|The app calls the API with the access token; the API validates it. Client credentials flow is used for service-to-service.
p2-47.qa: In the authorization code flow with PKCE, the app redirects the user to the identity provider with a code_challenge (a hash of a random code_verifier); the user logs in; the provider redirects back with a short-lived authorization code; the app exchanges the code plus the code_verifier at the token endpoint for tokens (ID token with OpenID Connect, access token, refresh token). PKCE proves the same app that started the flow is finishing it, so stolen codes are useless.
i: PKCE is recommended for all clients, including confidential ones (OAuth 2.1 makes it mandatory).
state parameter prevents CSRF; nonce protects the ID token from replay.
The implicit flow is deprecated; SPAs use code + PKCE or a backend-for-frontend.
Refresh token rotation detects token theft.
Machine-to-machine uses client credentials instead.
f: Why is the code exchanged on a back channel?
Tokens are not exposed in browser URLs or history.
What does the BFF pattern do?
A server-side component handles tokens and gives the SPA only a secure session cookie.

p2-48.a: A JWT stays valid until it expires even after the user clicks logout, because the server is stateless.|Fixes: short access-token lifetimes; revoke refresh tokens server-side on logout; a denylist of token ids (jti) checked in middleware until expiry; clear cookies; end the IdP session for SSO.|Also invalidate on password change or role change.|Situation: a [2024 security review] found that in one IRT module a JWT access token captured before logout could still call the APIs until it expired, [60 minutes] later.|Task: make logout really end access, without adding noticeable latency to every API call.|Action: I cut the access-token lifetime to [15 minutes]. On logout the server now revokes the refresh token, which is stored server-side, and writes the access token's jti to a denylist in ElastiCache (Redis) with a TTL equal to the token's remaining life. The JWT bearer OnTokenValidated event checks that denylist with one key lookup. Logout also clears the auth cookies and calls the identity provider's end-session endpoint so the SSO session ends too. I added a unit test and a Playwright test that replays an old token after logout and expects 401.|Result: the retest passed, old tokens are rejected immediately after logout, and the denylist check adds about [1 ms] per request. The fix went through review and the regulated release process.
p2-48.fu: Why not just use server-side sessions instead of JWT?::That works too, but the APIs are called by several services and scale out behind a load balancer. Keeping JWTs stateless and adding a small denylist only for logged-out tokens was the smaller, safer change.||What if Redis is unavailable?::We alert on it and fail closed for that check, returning 401 so the user logs in again, because accepting a revoked token is worse than an extra login. The short token lifetime limits exposure either way.||Why a TTL on denylist entries?::Once the token's own expiry passes, it is rejected anyway, so the entry can expire. That keeps the denylist small.
p2-48.qa: JWTs stay valid until expiry even after logout because the API validates them statelessly. In [2024] a security review found tokens in one IRT module still worked [60 minutes] after logout; I cut access-token lifetime to [15 minutes], revoked refresh tokens server-side, added a jti denylist in ElastiCache with TTL equal to the remaining lifetime checked in OnTokenValidated, cleared cookies and ended the IdP session. Old tokens were rejected immediately, at about [1 ms] per request.
i: Denylist only stores logged-out tokens, so it stays tiny and keeps APIs mostly stateless.
Fail closed if Redis is unavailable (401 and re-login), with alerting.
Also revoke on password change, role removal or account disable.
Tests: unit test for the event handler, Playwright test replaying an old token after logout expecting 401.
Alternatives: reference tokens with introspection, or server-side sessions; heavier for many services.
f: Why not just shorten tokens to 1 minute?
Constant refreshes add load and complexity; short tokens plus a denylist is a better balance.
What is the end-session endpoint?
The OpenID Connect logout endpoint that ends the SSO session at the identity provider.
wv: I balance security with performance and choose the smallest safe change.
I prove a security fix with automated tests, not just manual retest.

p2-49.a: Servers limit total request header size (IIS, Kestrel, load balancers, often 8 to 16 KB).|SSO tokens with many claims or groups, stored in cookies, can exceed it; chunked auth cookies add up across apps on the same domain.|Fixes: trim claims, store the session server-side and keep only a reference in the cookie, scope cookie domain and path, clean stale cookies; raising limits is a last resort.|Situation: in [2024] some users, mostly [study managers with access to many studies], got 'HTTP 400: the size of the request headers is too long' straight after SSO login, while other users were fine. We had [about 30] support tickets over [two weeks].|Task: find out why only some users failed and fix it permanently.|Action: I reproduced it with a test user given many role and study groups. ASP.NET Core cookie authentication was storing every role and group claim in the auth cookie and splitting it into [5] chunks of about [13 KB] in total. Together with other apps' cookies on the same parent domain, the Cookie header passed the [16 KB] request-header limit of the IIS/http.sys front end. I removed group and role claims from the cookie by storing the authentication ticket server-side through an ITicketStore, so the cookie holds only a session key, and loaded study-level permissions per request through claims transformation with caching. I also narrowed the cookie path and domain so sibling apps' cookies were not sent, and cleared old cookie names.|Result: the auth cookie fell from [about 13 KB to under 1 KB], affected users could log in again, and I added a regression test with a user in [200+] groups. We did not raise the server limits.
p2-49.fu: Why not just increase the header size limit?::It only moves the problem. The next user with more groups fails again, and every request carries a big cookie, which wastes bandwidth and exposes more data. Shrinking the cookie fixes the cause.||What is an ITicketStore?::An ASP.NET Core cookie-auth extension point that stores the authentication ticket server-side (for example in Redis or SQL) and puts only a key in the cookie.||Did loading permissions per request slow things down?::They are cached per user for a short time, so the cost was negligible, and permission changes take effect faster than with claims baked into a cookie.
p2-49.qa: Browsers send all cookies for a domain on every request, and servers cap total header size (IIS/http.sys around 16 KB in our setup); SSO auth cookies holding many role and group claims are chunked into several cookies and can exceed it, giving 400 "request header too long" for users in many groups. I fixed it by moving the auth ticket server-side with ITicketStore (cookie holds only a key), loading study permissions per request with cached claims transformation, and narrowing cookie domain and path, so the cookie dropped from [about 13 KB to under 1 KB].
i: Diagnosis: the pattern (only users with many studies) pointed to claim volume; a test user with many groups reproduced it.
Why not raise limits: the next user with more groups fails again, and every request carries kilobytes of cookie.
ITicketStore backed by [Redis/ElastiCache] with sliding expiry matching the session.
Claims transformation (IClaimsTransformation) adds permissions per request from a cache.
Result: tickets stopped, no user-visible change, released through the regulated process.
f: What is cookie chunking?
ASP.NET Core splits a large auth cookie into several cookies (.AspNetCore.CookiesC1, C2...) to stay under per-cookie size limits.
How did you verify the fix?
Test users with many groups in validation, header size measurements, and no new tickets after release.
wv: I look for the pattern behind "random" user problems before changing configuration.
I prefer fixing the root cause over raising a limit.

p2-50.a: A page opened with target=_blank gets window.opener and can redirect the original tab to a phishing page.|Fix: rel="noopener noreferrer" on links (modern browsers default noopener for _blank, but be explicit), and `window.open(url, '_blank', 'noopener')`.|Also set Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy.|I fixed this across the IRT UI.
p2-50.qa: Reverse tabnabbing is when a page opened with target="_blank" uses window.opener to navigate the original tab, for example to a fake login page, while the user is looking at the new tab. The fix is rel="noopener noreferrer" on links and the noopener feature in window.open, plus Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy; modern browsers default to noopener for target="_blank", but explicit is safer.
i: noopener sets window.opener to null; noreferrer also hides the Referer header.
COOP: same-origin isolates your browsing context group from cross-origin popups.
ESLint react/jsx-no-target-blank prevents regressions in React code.
I fixed [about 40] links in IRT in [2024] and enabled the lint rule (full story in Part 6).
f: Why does it matter in a clinical app?
A phishing redirect of a logged-in study manager's tab could steal credentials.
Do modern browsers fix it?
Most default _blank links to noopener, but window.open and older browsers still need explicit protection.

p2-51.a: Broken access control: check authorization per resource, not just per endpoint.|Injection: parameterised queries, validation.|Cryptographic failures: TLS everywhere, encrypt at rest, no secrets in code.|Security misconfiguration, vulnerable components (scan dependencies, SonarQube), logging and monitoring failures, SSRF.
p2-51.qa: For APIs the most important risks (OWASP API Security Top 10 2023) are broken object level authorization (accessing another study's data by changing an id), broken authentication, broken object property level authorization (over-posting, excessive data exposure), unrestricted resource consumption, broken function level authorization, SSRF, security misconfiguration and unsafe consumption of third-party APIs. I prevent them with per-object authorization checks, DTOs, rate limits, validation and hardened configuration.
i: BOLA: every query filtered by what the caller may access (resource-based authorization), never trusting ids from the client.
Input validation and parameterised queries for injection.
Limits: payload size, page size, rate limits, timeouts.
Security headers, HTTPS only, no stack traces, least-privilege service accounts.
Inventory and version APIs so old endpoints do not stay exposed.
f: What is BOLA in practice?
GET /api/studies/42/subjects works for a user who has no access to study 42 because the API only checked login.
How do you test for it?
Automated tests calling endpoints as a user without access, expecting 403 or 404.
